fixes.explanation: Nice thought, but the prophecy says otherwise. The LORD says He will gather all the nations for battle against Jerusalem, and "…the city will be captured…" (Zechariah 14:2). The verse doesn't say Jerusalem is left alone. It's a heavy part, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

Yes! "Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations, as He fights in the day of battle." (Zechariah 14:3). No army gets named as the one who steps in. The One who goes out is the LORD Himself. After a verse about a captured city, that's a turn worth noticing, friend.

That's it. "You will flee by My mountain valley, for it will extend to Azal." (Zechariah 14:5). The Mount of Olives is split in two, forming a great valley (Zechariah 14:4). The mountain splits and the valley becomes the way out. That's quite a hallway to have appear out of nowhere.

Yes! "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." (Zechariah 14:5). He arrives with company. The text doesn't tell us more than that, so I won't either. It comes right after the verse about fleeing through the valley.

Kings, huh? I like the royal energy, friend, but this verse doesn't list any. It says "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." (Zechariah 14:5). The ones with Him are called the holy ones, and the text stops there.

Correct. "…but when evening comes, there will be light." (Zechariah 14:7). It's a unique day known only to the LORD, without day or night. Evening shows up and the light shows up with it. That's not the usual order at all.

Yes. "…living water will flow out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the Eastern Sea and the other half toward the Western Sea, in summer and winter alike." (Zechariah 14:8). Half of it heads toward each sea. Any season, it keeps flowing. I've never had an oven that steady.

That's the word. "On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth…" (Zechariah 14:9). Not over one city or one land, but all the earth. The verse goes on, "…the LORD alone, and His name alone." (Zechariah 14:9).

Priest is a fine job, friend, but it isn't the word here. The verse says "On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth…" (Zechariah 14:9). King is the title, and it's King over all the earth, not just one corner of it. Priest doesn't appear in this verse.

Yes. "People will live there, and never again will there be an utter destruction. So Jerusalem will dwell securely." (Zechariah 14:11). Just before that, the city "…will be raised up and will remain in her place…" (Zechariah 14:10). Never again is a big promise, and the city dwells securely.

Yes. "…the wealth of all the surrounding nations will be collected—gold, silver, and apparel in great abundance." (Zechariah 14:14). That's gold, silver and clothing, piled up. It's in the same verse that says Judah will also fight at Jerusalem. I've never seen a cookie box that full.

Scattered, like crumbs off a cookie tray? I see the picture, friend, but the verse says the opposite. The wealth "…will be collected…" (Zechariah 14:14). Gathered up, not scattered, and the text names gold, silver and apparel in great abundance.

That's the turn. "Then all the survivors from the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts…" (Zechariah 14:16). Survivors from the very nations that came against Jerusalem are the ones going up to worship. And they go year after year.

Yes. They go up "…to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles." (Zechariah 14:16). The prophecy names it again in verses 18 and 19. So this feast is no side note here.

That's it. The text says "And should any of the families of the earth not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, then the rain will not fall on them." (Zechariah 14:17). The rain is what's held back. It's about families of the earth, not just one nation.

Manna is real in Scripture. The LORD promised bread from heaven for Israel (Exodus 16:4), and Israel called that bread manna (Exodus 16:31). But this verse isn't about manna. It says "…then the rain will not fall on them." (Zechariah 14:17).

Yes. "…the cooking pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). The everyday pots are put right alongside those bowls. Then verse 21 says every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of Hosts.

Water jars by a well sound lovely, friend, but they aren't in the verse. The text says the cooking pots "…will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). The comparison is to the bowls by the altar, not to anything out by the well.

A storeroom is a sensible guess, since that's where jars tend to live. But the verse says "…the cooking pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). The comparison is to the bowls before the altar, not to anything in storage.
